prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby changing the analysis of exporting, foreign direct investment, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My first choice is unchanged, but the exchange led me to narrow the citation and to change my alternatives. Melitz (2003) moved trade theory from representative industries to firms that differ in productivity and sort into exporting. This created a reallocation channel for the gains from trade and tied theory directly to firm-level data. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple then extended the framework to the choice between exporting and foreign direct investment. That extension turned the model into a working framework for empirical and quantitative trade work, which is why I keep Helpman on the ticket. The mechanism is a single, checkable discovery with a clear originator and more than twenty years of theoretical, structural and firm-level confirmation. After reading the colleagues' files, I now treat the citation as the claim to be defended. It should rest on selection into exporting and FDI and on the resulting reallocation. It should not claim all quantitative trade or any single welfare number. The round-1 exchange did not change my reading of the science. It changed how I would state the credit, and it moved B038 to the top of my alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made parallel contributions and are not on the ballot, and Hopenhayn-style selection models are precursors. A Melitz-Helpman citation therefore cannot do justice to everyone with a claim on the idea. Helpman's strongest independent case may lie in B013 or in earlier work, so the pairing could look assembled, and Helpman sits on two rival configurations. Krugman's 2008 prize covered the monopolistic-competition foundation that Melitz builds on, so the room left for a second trade award is a real question. Welfare gains from selection depend on specification. I also hold B041 and B038 to the same standard on magnitudes. If debated effect sizes do not undercut the China-shock finding, then specification-dependent welfare numbers should not undercut the selection mechanism, and the gap between the two cases is small. B038 now has the more convergent attribution among its supporters and a narrower, more defensible citation. I could not defend a claim that B041 is clearly ahead of it on science.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved B038 to Autor, Hanson and Dorn, replacing Katz with Dorn. He anchors the citation in trade exposure and local labour-market adjustment rather than the whole task framework. He now holds B013 as a close alternative because Helpman's overlap with B041 complicates the framing.
responses.response: His narrowed citation and his move to Dorn persuade me that B038 has the cleanest attribution of the empirical candidates. It also answers my earlier worry about how much of the task lineage the trio could claim. I agree with him that the Helpman overlap makes B013 and B041 rivals, not complements. I still keep B041 first, but only by a small margin. I apply the same standard to both sides. Debated magnitudes and shift-share scrutiny do not undermine the basic finding of persistent local adjustment costs, just as specification-dependent welfare numbers do not undermine the selection mechanism. For that reason I list B038 as my first alternative and no longer rank it outside my top choices.

responses.point: Krusell argues that B041's attribution is looser than Grossman-Helpman's because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited, and that B041 is the more direct successor to the new trade theory recognised in 2008. He treats B013 as a different question, why policy takes the form it does.
responses.response: I accept the attribution point. It is the main reason I narrow the citation and keep Melitz-alone as a fallback. I only partly accept the successor point. Melitz does build on the monopolistic-competition framework from the 2008 work, but the new object is selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms. That is a distinct channel, and it was introduced when firm-level data first became widely usable. I also agree that B013 is cleaner on credit and at least as mature. I rank it below B041 because its specific predictions have a mixed empirical record, while the firm-heterogeneity framework reshaped how trade is measured. Because Helpman cannot be credited on both entries, I keep B013 as the second alternative. The Committee would then have to choose which achievement to credit him for, and I do not think the exchange has settled that choice.

responses.point: Andersson proposed Melitz alone for B041 because Melitz is the clear originator and a single name expresses the core discovery most cleanly. He accepts Helpman through the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension as a fair reading of the ballot, but he finds the trade candidates harder to settle than the bargaining case.
responses.response: I take Melitz alone seriously as the most defensible form if the Committee judges the extension derivative. I still prefer Melitz and Helpman, with the citation worded to include foreign direct investment so that Helpman's share rests on something specific. Dropping Helpman would credit the idea but not the step that made it usable at scale. This is a judgement about attribution that I cannot verify independently. If members read the extension as secondary, Melitz alone is my fallback rather than a switch to a different configuration. I also agree that the trade space is harder to settle than the bargaining case. That is a point about uncertainty over credit and prior-prize overlap. It is not a point about the quality of B001, which I now leave out of my alternatives only because I have to choose two.

responses.point: Friberg ranked B041 fourth and B030 first. He says credit among Melitz, Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Helpman is contested, that Redding's work is later, and that welfare gains from selection depend on specification. He also says familiarity with trade may inflate views of the field.
responses.response: His attribution objection is the strongest case against my choice and I have built it into the narrowed citation. I agree on Redding. No one proposes him and I leave him out. I also take the familiarity warning as applying to me, since firm-level trade is a literature I know well, and I count it against my own confidence. Where we differ is on whether B030 is clearly more settled than B041. Both have about two decades or more of use. Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes is the cleaner attribution and is a methods contribution with wide use in antitrust and applied fields. Melitz is a conceptual advance, with firm-level evidence supporting it. Under common criteria I weigh a substantive change in how a field understands the economy somewhat above a well-attributed tool. This is a close call, and I do not think it is decisive.

uncertainties: How far the credit for firm heterogeneity extends beyond Melitz and Helpman, to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the ballot, and whether the Committee would prefer Melitz alone.
Whether the 2008 prize leaves room for either trade configuration, and whether Helpman should be credited through B041 or B013.
Whether the Committee will weigh B038's debated magnitudes and shift-share scrutiny and B041's specification-dependent welfare estimates by one common standard.
Whether my own familiarity with trade and firm-level work, and my trust in the Melitz-Helpman pairing, are inflating my confidence relative to B038, whose attribution has converged.

Whether the Committee reads prior-prize proximity as a matter of the same contribution or only the same theme, for 2008 (B013 and B041), 2022 (B012), earlier game-theory prizes (B001) and recent labour and technology prizes (B038).
My assessments rely on the supplied evidence and general knowledge, without independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Melitz, Helpman or Redding is apparent from the supplied profile. None of the B038 or B013 names is among my listed co-authors. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and have co-authored with Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, and I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. This may affect how I read their arguments, and I have tried to answer them on the merits. Friberg's work in trade and industrial organisation is adjacent to B041, and he and Boppart ranked B041 fourth. I also wrote the round-1 chair summary in this simulation. My own first choice was B041, and that summary was meant to give all positions equal weight. My research on social mobility is relevant to B002, which I do not prefer. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
